analysis.one_liner: Phases out fracking nationwide, banning new permits immediately and all fracking by 2025.
analysis.headline: The fracking ban died in committee without a hearing or vote, after drawing only two Senate supporters.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would immediately block federal agencies from approving any new fracking operations or fracked oil and gas infrastructure like pipelines and export terminals. It would revoke permits for existing fracked wells within 2,500 feet of homes, schools, or other buildings, order a national survey of all fracked wells, and ban fracking entirely on all US land, onshore and offshore, starting in 2025. It would also create a committee to recommend how to protect workers and communities in oil- and gas-producing regions as the industry winds down.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near fracked wells — over 17 million Americans live within a mile of a well or related facility, per the bill's own findings — would gain cleaner air and water and less risk of health harms the bill links to fracking. Workers and communities in oil and gas regions were promised a transition planning process, though with no guaranteed funding attached.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near fracked wells and gas infrastructure

how_it_helps.text: Bans new fracking permits and new fracked-gas infrastructure — pipelines, LNG export terminals, gas power plants — by barring federal agencies from approving their expansion.
Revokes permits on February 1, 2021 for any fracked well operating within 2,500 feet of a home, school, or other inhabited structure, forcing those wells to stop producing.
Bans hydraulic fracturing entirely on all onshore and offshore US land beginning January 1, 2025.
Requires the EPA to survey all US oil and gas wells to identify where fracking is used, including how close each well is to homes and schools and any known health and safety violations.

Creates a Just Transition Committee at the Labor Department, including organized labor and community representatives, to recommend how to protect the health, safety, and prosperity of oil- and gas-producing regions during the phaseout.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose the ability to drill new fracked wells, build pipelines, or open export terminals, and wells near homes would shut down within about a year. Fracking states — Texas, Pennsylvania, North Dakota, Oklahoma and others — would lose production, jobs, and tax revenue, and consumers could face higher energy prices unless renewables and efficiency scaled up fast enough to replace fracked gas, which supplied a large share of US electricity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and fracking-region workers

drawbacks.text: A 2025 ban on fracking would cut off the dominant method of US natural gas production — the industry projected up to 95% of new gas wells would be fracked — risking higher energy prices and electricity shortfalls if wind, solar, and storage did not expand fast enough.
Revoking permits for wells near homes within about a year of enactment would shut down producing wells abruptly, hitting oil and gas workers and royalty-receiving landowners immediately.

The Just Transition Committee only issues recommendations; the bill attaches no guaranteed income, pension, healthcare, training, or funding for displaced workers or producing regions, even though its own findings call for those guarantees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and climate case is substantial: the bill documents water contamination risks, methane's heat-trapping power, and millions of people living close to wells. But the transition plan is weak — the Just Transition Committee produces advice, not funded guarantees — so workers and towns in fracking regions would bear the loss without strong protection. The immediate 2,500-foot permit revocation is abrupt. A phased ban paired with real funding for affected workers and communities would have been a stronger design.

outcome.mechanism: Sanders introduced it in the Senate in January 2020, it was referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and the committee never held a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Bernie Sanders introduced the Fracking Ban Act in the Senate on January 28, 2020, with Jeff Merkley as the cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the day it was introduced.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers keep full access to fracking, new pipelines, and export terminals. Fracking-state workers and local economies also avoid disruption. Residents near wells keep the pollution risks the bill aimed to remove.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers and fracking regions

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fracking Ban Act on January 28, 2020.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the sole cosponsor in the Senate.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's entire recorded Senate support was one Independent sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, with no Republican support recorded.

industries.note: The ban would end fracking entirely by 2025 and block new fracked wells and infrastructure immediately, eliminating the industry's primary drilling method. Its output also creates the pollution and health risks near homes the bill targets.
New pipelines, gas storage, and LNG or oil export terminals would be barred from federal permitting, freezing infrastructure growth built to move fracked fuel.
New ethane cracker plants, which turn fracked gas liquids into plastics, would be blocked from federal permits.
With fracked gas phased out, electricity demand shifts toward wind, solar, and storage, which the bill's findings call commercially ready and cost-competitive.
